Orbit response¶

Parametric twiss example

This notebook requires knowledge of GTPSA.jl because it uses twiss with as_taylor_series=true.

using SciBmad
using CairoMakie
set_theme!(theme_latexfonts()) # Set plotting package theme to LaTeX
include("../../lattices/RCSV5S0.jl");
tw = twiss(ring)

# Plot the betas
f = Figure(fontsize=22, size=(800,500));
ax = Axis(f[1, 1], xlabel="s [m]", ylabel="Beta Functions");
lines!(ax, tw.s, tw.beta1, label=L"\beta_1"); 
lines!(ax, tw.s, tw.beta2, label=L"\beta_2");
axislegend(position=:lt);
display(f);

# Let's see the linear closed orbit response as a function of
# e.g. qf_1 y_alignment and b0_1 tilt (2 PARAMETERS)
const DPARAMS1 = Descriptor(6, 1, 2, 1) # 6 dynamic variables to 1st order, 2 parameters to 1st order
Δk = params(DPARAMS1)
qf_1.y_offset = Δk[1] # make y_offset a parameter
b0_1.tilt = Δk[2]      # make tilt a parameter
tw = twiss(ring; GTPSA_descriptor=DPARAMS1, as_taylor_series=true)

# Closed orbit is now a Taylor series in the parameters:
# E.g. at the first element:
tw.y[1]

TPS64{GTPSA.Dynamic}:
Descriptor(NV=6, MO=1, NP=2, PO=1)
 COEFFICIENT             ORDER   EXPONENTS
-3.4019914795092449E-01    1     0 0  0 0  0 0  7^1
-3.4327120607789981E-02    1     0 0  0 0  0 0  8^1

This says that \(\frac{\partial y_{co}}{\partial(\textrm{y\_offset})} = -3.4019914795092449\times 10^{-1}\) and \(\frac{\partial y_{co}}{\partial(\textrm{tilt})} = -3.5426682007214952\times 10^{-2}\). See the orbit response around the ring:

dy_dy_offset = map(x->x[[0,0,0,0,0,0,1]], tw.y)
dy_dtilt = map(x->x[[0,0,0,0,0,0,0,1]], tw.y)

# Plot the response around the ring:
f = Figure(fontsize=22, size=(800,500));
ax = Axis(f[1, 1], xlabel="s [m]");
lines!(ax, tw.s, dy_dy_offset, label=L"\frac{\partial y_{co}}{\partial(\textrm{y\_offset})}\ \textrm{(Exact)}"); # L".." specifies a LaTeX string
lines!(ax, tw.s, dy_dtilt, label=L"\frac{\partial y_{co}}{\partial(\textrm{tilt})}\ \textrm{(Exact)}");
axislegend(position=:lt);
display(f);

Now let’s compare to finite differencing:

# First get rid of TPSA parameters in ring:
scalarize!(ring)

# Now set up finite differences:
step = 1e-6

# First dy/dy_offset
qf_1.y_offset = step
b0_1.tilt = 0
t = twiss(ring)
# scalar gets zeroth order part
dy_dy_offset_FD = scalar.(t.y)/step

# Now dy/dtilt:
qf_1.y_offset = 0
b0_1.tilt = step
t = twiss(ring)
dy_dtilt_FD = scalar.(t.y)/step

# And plot:
# Plot the response around the ring:
f = Figure(fontsize=22, size=(800,500));
ax = Axis(f[1, 1], xlabel="s [m]");
lines!(ax, t.s, dy_dy_offset_FD, label=L"\frac{\partial y_{co}}{\partial(\textrm{y\_offset})}\ \textrm{(Finite differences)}"); # L".." specifies a LaTeX string
lines!(ax, t.s, dy_dtilt_FD, label=L"\frac{\partial y_{co}}{\partial(\textrm{tilt})}\ \textrm{(Finite differences)}");
axislegend(position=:lt);
display(f);

Finite differences is usually ok for first order derivatives, but suffers significant error beyond that. Thanks to SciBmad’s automatic differentiability, we can exactly compute the nonlinear derivatives. Simply specify a higher order for the GTPSA Descriptor and follow the same procedure above.
